chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abbad ibn Shuayb said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: 'The one performing tayammum does not lead the prayer of a congregation that is performing wudu.' (362) 23 And - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad from his father from Ibn al-Mughira from al-Sakuni from Ja'far from his father (peace be upon them both) who said: 'The one performing tayammum does not lead those performing wu in prayer, nor does the one with palsy lead the healthy.'

If it is said: 'The apparent meaning of these two narrations is that it is not permissible for the one performing tayammum to lead those performing wu in any way, so why did you interpret it as disliked (karamah) rather than forbidden (haram)?' We said: 'We did so only because many other narrations have come indicating the permissibility of this, so we needed to reconcile between them. Among those is what he narrated:'
ai.seo_question: Can the one performing tayammum lead the prayer of those performing wudu?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the fiqh of *imamah* (leadership in prayer), specifically whether a person performing *tayammum* (dry ablution due to lack of water) can lead those performing *wudu* (water ablution). Al-Tusi explains that while the apparent meaning of the hadith suggests prohibition, scholars interpret it as *karahah* (dislike) to harmonize it with other narrations that permit the practice, reflecting the Shia method of reconciling seemingly contradictory texts through contextual analysis.
